title: My Daily Brief
overview: Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman US authorities suspect of spying for China, and President Trump suggested Apple's Tim Cook as his replacement. Trump also said the US no longer needs a deal with Iran and redirected Vice President Vance toward Democratic-run states, while US envoys met Putin and Zelenskyy after Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi. Other stories include a global Microsoft 365 outage, a deadly building collapse in Brooklyn, oil price moves, and local and Korean news.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after affair reports; CFO Colette Kress named interim chief
stories.summary: Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and led it since, resigned as president, CEO and board member effective immediately on Thursday. The resignation followed reports of affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US authorities suspect of spying for China, and another with Kimberly Powell, a vice president who reported directly to him. Reuters later reported a third relationship with another employee. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO and director Harvey Jones becomes board chair while the board searches internally and externally for a permanent successor. Nvidia says it has no reason to believe national security or confidential information was compromised, China denies the spying allegation, and earnings are still due on Nov. 17.
key_facts: Huang resigned effective immediately on Thursday, ending a 33-year tenure; Kress, CFO since 2013, is interim CEO.
Harvey Jones, former Synopsys CEO, was named Nvidia's first board chair.
Shares fell about 13% at the open and closed down 4.3% on Thursday, per The Guardian; it put the day's loss at more than $180bn and the week's at around $490bn.
Law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz is conducting the board's independent investigation into the Alice Huang relationship.
Nvidia's Q3 fiscal 2027 earnings release remains scheduled for Nov. 17.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian gave a detailed timeline, noted that the board's statement left out the scandal, and covered market losses, Trump's Tim Cook post and the Reuters report of a third affair. The Verge collected reactions from tech leaders such as Musk, Tim Sweeney and David Heinemeier Hansson, many of whom called the resignation a rushed overreaction.

The Korea Herald and Axios focused on business continuity and Huang's importance to the AI boom. Axios cited Wall Street sources who said his exit could threaten an 'AI bubble' and predicted continued congressional scrutiny. The Korea Herald pointed to the impact on Korean suppliers Samsung and SK hynix.

Fox Business led with Musk saying it would be 'an honor' to hire Huang, and covered analyst downgrades, Megaspeed's statement on export-control compliance and China's denial. Reason's podcast treated the episode as Huang being 'honeypotted' by a suspected spy.

disputed: Whether Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset: US authorities suspect it, and China calls the accusation 'slander.'
Whether any company secrets or national security information were compromised; Nvidia says it has no reason to believe so.
The identity and details of the third alleged relationship reported by Reuters.
Who will become permanent CEO.
stories.why: Nvidia supplies most of the chips behind the AI boom, so a sudden leadership change touches markets, AI investment and US-China tech security.

stories.headline: Microsoft 365 outage disrupts Outlook, Teams and Copilot worldwide
stories.summary: A widespread outage on Thursday stopped many users worldwide from reaching Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive and Copilot. Microsoft first cited elevated infrastructure load, then said the load came from many servers unexpectedly becoming unavailable after failing automated health checks, not from more traffic. The company paused deployments, redistributed traffic, restarted servers and tested an alternative health-check method. It said configuration updates were a potential cause still under investigation, and by Thursday evening servers were beginning to return to service.
key_facts: Downdetector logged nearly 130,000 Outlook problem reports just after 1 p.m. ET.
Microsoft says the incident (MO1550821) began at 1:26 p.m. ET and could affect users in any region.
A separate Teams outage in the Americas earlier Thursday ran from 9:45 to 10:53 a.m. ET.
DW reported that Microsoft 365 connectors used by OpenAI and Anthropic were also affected.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian, The Verge and Al Jazeera tracked Microsoft's status updates step by step. The Guardian added an RMIT engineering professor who described a 'cascading' failure from misconfiguration and urged better testing and backup plans.
BleepingComputer gave the most technical detail, including incident IDs and the earlier Teams outage. DW and WSOC focused on the scale of user reports and the effects on users.

disputed: The root cause: Microsoft named configuration updates as a potential cause but had not confirmed it.
Whether the earlier Teams incident is related to the later outage.
When full service will be restored.
stories.why: Many businesses depend on Microsoft 365, so outages like this show the risk of relying on a single cloud provider.

stories.headline: Trump says US doesn't need an Iran deal and redirects Vance to Democratic-run states
stories.summary: In a Truth Social post on Thursday, President Trump wrote that 'we don't need a deal with Iran,' saying the US has Iran's money and 'their Strait.' He told Vice President JD Vance, who had been leading efforts to restart negotiations, to give his 'complete and total attention' to what Trump called corruption and crime in Democratic-run cities and states. The post came about a week after large Republican midterm losses, which Vance has attributed to the war that the US and Israel began in February. Stocks fell and oil prices rose after the post.
key_facts: Trump wrote: 'We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed.'
He named Minnesota, California and Illinois as 'poorly run, corrupt disasters.'
The war began in late February and is in its ninth month; major strikes have largely stopped for several months.
Vance said after the midterms: 'The reason we lost is the war.'

perspectives.framing: The Guardian described the move as normalising a stalemate and sidelining Vance from the main foreign policy issue of his vice presidency. It detailed his contacts with mediators in Qatar and Pakistan and his statement blaming the war for the midterm losses.

CNBC and Axios connected the post to the midterm defeat, the war's unpopularity and market reactions. CNBC described it as an attempt to 'flip the script' on corruption, an issue that favoured Democrats in the election.

The Daily Caller presented the move as a reassignment to fighting fraud. It highlighted Vance's existing fraud task force and its reported findings in several states, and linked to a White House official's criticism of 'establishment ghouls' blaming Vance's peace efforts.

disputed: Trump's claims of billions of dollars stolen monthly in blue states, and that the budget could be balanced by stopping it, are his assertions and were not verified in the articles.
Whether diplomatic contacts with Iran will continue through Kushner and Witkoff.
Whether the US 'has' the Strait, given reports of shipping being hit.
stories.why: Dropping the push for a deal could prolong the war and keep energy prices high.

stories.headline: Trump suggests Apple's Tim Cook as Nvidia's next CEO
stories.summary: After Jensen Huang's resignation, President Trump posted that 'there is only one man' to replace him, Apple executive chair Tim Cook, adding 'A Legend replaces a Legend!' Cook stepped down as Apple CEO on Sept. 1 and remains executive chairman. Trump did not say whether Cook was interested, and some outlets were unsure whether he was serious. Yale's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld had separately named Cook as a possible candidate.
key_facts: Trump called Huang someone 'who has done a fantastic job.'
Cook led Apple from 2011 to 2026; John Ternus is now Apple's CEO.
Nvidia's board is considering both internal and external candidates.
Trump had defended Huang on Monday, saying he believed Huang did not know of the woman's alleged intelligence ties.

perspectives.framing: TechCrunch and Axios treated the endorsement with some scepticism, questioning whether Trump meant it as a joke. They noted he did not address the scandal and cited Sonnenfeld's similar suggestion.

Fox Business and the Daily Caller reported the endorsement straightforwardly. The Daily Caller added Trump's ties to Cook, Apple's $500 billion US investment, a Bloomberg report via social media of a DOJ probe into Alice Huang, and an allegation that she helped move $7.5 billion in chips to China. Fox noted that no evidence has been publicly established that secrets were obtained.

disputed: Whether Cook has any interest in the role.
The Daily Caller's claim that Alice Huang used the relationship to move more than $7.5 billion in Nvidia chips to China is unverified in the other coverage.
The reported DOJ probe into Alice Huang over Super Micro products was cited from a social media post of a Bloomberg report.
stories.why: Presidential involvement in a private company's succession is unusual and may affect how Nvidia's board approaches the search.

stories.headline: US envoys meet Putin, then Zelenskyy, after Abu Dhabi talks end without a ceasefire
stories.summary: Two days of US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi ended Wednesday without a ceasefire but with agreement on a large prisoner exchange, the exact numbers still to be set. Envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff then met Vladimir Putin in Moscow for about two hours. Putin kept his territorial demands for four annexed regions and said any European troops in Ukraine would be legitimate targets. Witkoff said Europeans would join the next round of talks, and the envoys went on to Dublin to brief Zelenskyy at a European Political Community summit. Zelenskyy separately said Ukraine faces 'systematic' restrictions on SpaceX's Starshield service.
key_facts: The Abu Dhabi talks were the first direct Russia-Ukraine talks in nine months.
Russia said a prisoner exchange could happen within two to three weeks.
Putin said European troops in Ukraine would mean 'the war would resume immediately.'
More than 40 European leaders met in Dublin; the EU has not named a single negotiator.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian, NPR, PBS (AP) and Al Jazeera emphasised Putin's hard line, European unease about Russia reframing the talks as a discussion of European security, and Kaja Kallas's objections. PBS noted Trump's past moves that dismayed Kyiv, and Al Jazeera focused on hybrid attacks across Europe.

DW stressed the humanitarian outcome and quoted Ukrainian experts who were sceptical that the upbeat official statements reflect real progress. The BBC highlighted the Starlink/Starshield disruption and Putin's proposed local humanitarian truce.

disputed: Who ordered the Starshield restrictions, and why, remains unclear.
Whether Europe will appoint a single representative.
Final numbers for the prisoner exchange.
Whether a deal is possible by year-end: Ukrainian negotiators are hopeful, while experts are doubtful.
stories.why: These talks are the most active diplomacy in months on a war approaching its fifth year, with consequences for European security.

stories.headline: Brooklyn building collapse kills eight; city records show earlier inspection concerns
stories.summary: A three-story 1930s apartment building in Flatbush, Brooklyn, collapsed into a neighbouring excavation site shortly after 4 p.m. Wednesday, killing eight people, including two children and two construction workers. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said 18 people were injured, including four firefighters. The FDNY finished searching the site Thursday afternoon and handed it to police and the Department of Buildings. The city has opened an investigation and is inspecting about 100 sites linked to the same five entities. Newsweek reported that a March pre-construction inspection rated the building's north wall 'poor' with visible cracks.
key_facts: 8 dead: 6 found at the scene and 2 who died in hospital.
About 250 first responders worked the site, and a pregnant woman was rescued from the rubble.
The DOB issued a stop-work order at the adjacent site on March 20; work resumed in violation of it and was allowed to continue on May 8.
The cause has not been determined.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian and NPR focused on the rescue operation, the human toll and officials' statements, with NPR presenting a photo essay.
The BBC centred residents' grief and the area's immigrant community. Newsweek examined permit and inspection records pointing to earlier warnings about the building's condition.
The Daily Caller and Washington Examiner covered the death toll and rescue work. The Daily Caller profiled Jose Luis Caguana, an Ecuadorian worker who was killed.

disputed: The cause of the collapse.
Injury counts differ slightly between reports (17 vs 18).
The developers and the engineer had not responded to Newsweek.
stories.why: The collapse raises questions about how construction next to older buildings is overseen in New York City.

stories.headline: Oil rises after Trump's Iran comments; South Korean import prices fall
stories.summary: Oil prices rose Thursday after President Trump said the US did not need a deal with Iran, raising doubts that the war would end soon. Brent rose 1.9% to $94.48, though both benchmarks remain sharply down for November. Analysts quoted by CNBC said markets may have priced in peace too early and warned that renewed Iranian attacks on shipping could push prices higher. Separately, the Bank of Korea said October import prices fell 1.8% on a stronger won and lower oil prices.
key_facts: WTI rose 2% to $88.19.
WTI is down 16% and Brent down 20% in November.
South Korea's import price index fell 1.8% month-on-month in October, while export prices rose 0.7%.

perspectives.framing: CNBC framed the rise through market analysts' views on the security premium and the blockade. Yonhap reported the Korean data in a straightforward, data-driven way.

disputed: Whether Iran will respond with further attacks on shipping.
stories.why: Energy prices affect inflation and household costs worldwide.

stories.headline: South Carolina regulators monitor Silfab Solar as it resumes equipment testing
stories.summary: Staff from South Carolina's Department of Environmental Services toured Silfab Solar's Fort Mill plant Thursday and will stay on site for several weeks while the company restarts commissioning of its solar-cell equipment. The state had earlier asked Silfab to halt commissioning after two chemical leaks this year. A court case over whether the operations are allowed under York County zoning is still pending, and some neighbours want Silfab to wait for the ruling.
key_facts: Two chemical leaks occurred earlier this year.
Oversight will continue until commissioning is complete.

perspectives.framing: Local TV stations reported the regulatory oversight and noted neighbours' concerns and the pending lawsuit.

disputed: Whether the operations comply with York County zoning is before a court.
stories.why: Nearby residents face potential safety risks while the legal question is unresolved.

stories.headline: NC lawmaker plans bill to split Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools and allow board recalls
stories.summary: Union County state Rep. David Willis says he is drafting legislation to break up Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools and allow recall elections for its board members. The proposal follows the firing of Dr. Crystal Hill and several investigations into the district. Willis acknowledges a split would likely take years because of lawsuits and pushback, and he wants a study committee to work out the new districts' geography and finances. CMS has not commented.
key_facts: CMS is North Carolina's second-largest school district.
The three at-large board seats are up next year; district seats are not up until 2029.

perspectives.framing: Local outlets relayed Willis's reasoning and quotes, noted the obstacles he acknowledges, and reported that CMS had not responded.

disputed: Whether the bill has enough legislative support to pass.
stories.why: The proposal could reshape governance of a large urban school district.

stories.headline: North Korea rejects G7 call for denuclearization
stories.summary: North Korean Foreign Minister Choe Son-hui rejected a G7 foreign ministers' statement from Paris that called for North Korea's complete denuclearization. In a statement carried by state media, she said Pyongyang's 'will for nuclear possession' is steadfast and accused the G7 of double standards because some members hold nuclear weapons. She also criticised the US, Britain and Japan.
key_facts: Choe called nuclear weapons the 'most powerful guarantee' of sovereignty.
UN Security Council resolutions ban North Korea's nuclear and missile programs.

perspectives.framing: Yonhap and The Korea Herald reported Choe's remarks directly, giving the context of the G7 statement and the UN resolutions.

stories.why: The statement signals that North Korea has no intention of negotiating away its nuclear arsenal.
